evidence: Table 2-2 row 'Prefill: regime verdict': "weight-only arithmetic intensity ~9.2K FLOP/byte — an upper bound that omits the ~24 GB KV write; including it, ~7,850 FLOP/byte (Ch 8) — both > ridge ~295 → on the compute-bound side of the roofline". Arithmetic: 1.29 PFLOP ÷ 140 GB = 9,214 FLOP/byte; 1.29 PFLOP ÷ (140 + 24.1) GB = 7,861 FLOP/byte ≈ 7,850.
issue: The cell as written is internally ordered correctly (weight-only first, then 'including it'), but the sentence structure makes 'upper bound that omits…' modify 9.2K and 'including it' modify 7,850 — which is correct — yet 7,850 < 9,200, so 'including it' reduces the ratio. A reader skimming 'both > ridge 295' may conclude 7,850 > 9,200 or that including KV raises intensity. More importantly, the sentence 'including it, ~7,850 FLOP/byte' in isolation reads as if including the KV write gives 7,850 as an *increase* over 9.2K. The correct reading is that 7,850 is the *reduced* (still above-ridge) intensity once KV-write bytes are added to the denominator. This ordering error recurs in Fig. 2.2's caption on page 28 which says 'counting that write puts the same point at ~7,850 FLOP/byte — still well right of the ridge' (also correct but similarly ambiguous in direction).
fix_instruction: Rewrite the cell as: 'weight-only arithmetic intensity = 1.29 PFLOP ÷ 140 GB ≈ 9,214 FLOP/byte (upper bound, omits KV write); adding the ~24 GB KV write to the denominator gives ≈ 7,861 FLOP/byte — lower but still ≫ ridge ~295.' Make the direction explicit: including KV write *lowers* intensity.

evidence: Preface, 'Evidence boundary' paragraph: "The four terms below are the ones a reader meets most often… Axis 3 also takes SCENARIO-DERIVED, MODELED and UNMEASURED (all five Axis-3 values are listed in the Axis note below); each term names its axis, and each is the same item as the matching value defined further down this section." The very next parenthetical says: "…HYPOTHESIS (Axis 2, epistemic status) — reasoned but not yet validated (with UNRESOLVED for questions the book leaves open), used where mechanism is argued without measurement."
issue: UNRESOLVED (an Axis-2 epistemic status) is introduced inside a parenthetical attached to the HYPOTHESIS (Axis-2) term within a paragraph that is discussing Axis-3 measurement statuses and claims to list 'all five Axis-3 values' in the Axis note. The Axis note lists five Axis-3 values (ANALYTICAL, SCENARIO-DERIVED, MODELED, MEASURED, UNMEASURED) but UNRESOLVED is an Axis-2 value, not an Axis-3 value. The paragraph's mixed-parenthetical presentation makes it appear as if UNRESOLVED belongs to Axis 3. The enumeration of 'four terms below' is itself correct (MEASURED, ANALYTICAL, ILLUSTRATIVE, HYPOTHESIS = 4), but the axis attribution of UNRESOLVED in this paragraph is confusing given the explicit warning against mixing axes.
fix_instruction: Move the UNRESOLVED mention so it is clearly within the Axis-2 discussion (or delete it from this parenthetical and rely on the full definition later). Ensure the sentence 'all five Axis-3 values are listed in the Axis note below' is not immediately followed by an Axis-2 value in a parenthetical.

evidence: §3.1.1 orientation box: "It is the book's coverage of the 2026 alternative-inference frontier; the core dense/MoE/KV thread resumes in §3.2 (Mental Model). Read now for the frontier signal, or skip to §3.2 and return through the cross-references in Appendix A §9A." The text also says (page 59): "§2.1.2 (latent video) and §3.1.1 (diffusion/LLaDA-style) carry the extension." And (page 61): "read the two as one treatment."
issue: The orientation box on page 60 tells the reader that §2.1.2 and §3.1.1 should be read 'as one treatment' — but §2.1.2 (page 59–60) covers whole-clip latent *video* generation (Wan2.2) while §3.1.1 (page 61) covers *diffusion/LLaDA-style* language generation. These are two different alternative-inference mechanisms with different execution schedules, not one treatment. The cross-reference on page 11 (line '(§2.1.2; §3.1.1 and Appendix A §9A)') lumps them together as if they are the same subject. A reader expecting 'one treatment' will find two distinctly scoped sub-sections.
fix_instruction: Change 'read the two as one treatment' to 'read the two as a paired treatment of non-autoregressive and whole-clip generation respectively, together with Appendix A §9A' — or remove the 'one treatment' claim and list them as complementary rather than identical.

evidence: Page 146, closing paragraph of §7.3.3: "Read every '8-bit' KV figure in this book as FP8 raw byte-halving (one payload byte per K/V element, exactly 2× against FP16)… the realized per-token footprint depends on the engine version… [DERIVED]".
issue: The [DERIVED] tag stands alone without an Axis-1 provenance tag. The Preface evidence boundary (page xv) states: 'A label pair always takes one item from each of the first two axes, e.g. [1P][DERIVED] or [canonical scenario][DERIVED].' This paragraph carries only [DERIVED] with no provenance tag. The same pattern recurs: page 137 ends '[1P][FACT] for the configuration; [DERIVED] for the storage' (the second should be [1P][DERIVED]); page 119 in Ch. 6 uses a bare [DERIVED] after a [canonical scenario][DERIVED] pair. Each bare [DERIVED] lacks its provenance counterpart.
fix_instruction: Add the appropriate Axis-1 provenance to every bare [DERIVED] tag: [canonical scenario][DERIVED] for canonical-scenario arithmetic, [1P][DERIVED] for arithmetic on first-party inputs, or [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] for non-canonical examples. Apply recurrence sweep across Chs. 6–8.

evidence: Preface, §'Hardware is a generic stand-in': "the H100 GPU's 0.989 PFLOPS BF16 dense tensor-core peak and 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, with an 8×H100 host used as the canonical deployment unit — because arithmetic needs concrete anchors."
issue: These are quantitative hardware constants (0.989 PFLOPS, 3.35 TB/s) presented in the Preface without any provenance label. The same values are properly labeled [1P][FACT] in Table 2-2 (page 30) and Table 4-2 (page 74). The Preface states labels run 'from Part I onward' and that front-matter production metadata is exempt — but hardware constants are not production metadata; they are load-bearing quantitative claims. The labeling rule says 'Every load-bearing quantitative claim carries Axes 1 and 2 as an inline pair' while also saying 'front-matter and production metadata — a page count, the edition date — are not load-bearing quantitative claims.' Hardware specs used as arithmetic anchors are load-bearing. The Preface itself says 'The rule runs from Part I onward' — but the H100 numbers in the Preface are identical to those the rule covers in Chs. 2 and 4, creating an inconsistency where the same fact is unlabeled here and labeled there.
fix_instruction: Add [1P][FACT] to the H100 BF16 peak and HBM bandwidth figures in the Preface, or explicitly note in the reading-conventions paragraph that hardware constants quoted as exemplars in front matter carry their labels from the chapter where they are load-bearing (Ch. 2/4).

evidence: Page 145, MXFP4 sensitivity paragraph: "In a 640 GB aggregate pool, a fixed 64 GB runtime reserve leaves 536.75625 GB of KV budget (640 − 39.24375 − 64 = 536.75625 GB)."
issue: The arithmetic checks: 640 − 39.24375 − 64 = 536.75625 ✓. However the prose says the 64 GB runtime reserve 'leaves' 536.76 GB — but the 64 GB is itself one of the three terms being subtracted. The phrase 'a fixed 64 GB runtime reserve leaves 536.76 GB of KV budget' can be read as: (after subtracting weights AND reserve) the KV budget remains. But 640 − 39.24375 = 600.7625, and then − 64 = 536.75625. The subtraction of the 64 GB reserve is correct, but the prose construction 'a fixed 64 GB runtime reserve leaves…' implies the reserve is *being* left (i.e., added back), when in fact it is being subtracted alongside the weights. The standard Ch. 7 formula is 640 − 140 − 64 = 436, where 64 is subtracted separately from weights — here 640 − 39.24 − 64 = 536.76 follows the same pattern, but the English is ambiguous about which term is 'leaving'.
fix_instruction: Rewrite as: 'After subtracting the MXFP4 weights (39.24375 GB) and the fixed 64 GB runtime reserve, the KV budget is 640 − 39.24375 − 64 = 536.75625 GB.'

evidence: Page 10, §1.2 Mental Model: "for non-AR generation the same reasoning runs on model evaluations instead of output tokens, and §2.1.2 (latent video) and §3.1.1 (diffusion/LLaDA-style) carry the extension."
issue: The cross-reference labels §2.1.2 as '(latent video)'. The actual section heading on page 59 is 'The work unit changes with the generator'. While the section does discuss latent video as its example, the parenthetical label does not match the section title, making it harder for a reader using the TOC or section headings to locate the referenced content. The convention elsewhere in the book (e.g., '§7.3 (mechanism inventory)') uses paraphrased topic labels that are clearly descriptive; '(latent video)' is a topic label but does not match any heading.
fix_instruction: Either use the actual section title ('§2.1.2 (the work unit changes with the generator)') or a more general label ('§2.1.2 (non-text generation)') that the reader can match to the heading.

evidence: Figure label on page 9: "figure 1.1: The KV cache…". Figure label on page 11: "figure 1.2: How a token travels…". Cross-reference in Fig. 1.1 caption: "The full token-travel pipeline is in Fig 1.2 and the end-to-end pipeline in Fig 2.1". Cross-reference in Fig. 1.2 caption: "the full read-side mechanics and the iterative loop are shown in Fig 2.1".
issue: The figure labels use the form 'figure N.M' (lowercase word, period separator: 'figure 1.1', 'figure 1.2') but the cross-references within captions use 'Fig N.M' (abbreviated, space separator: 'Fig 1.2', 'Fig 2.1'). The Preface's cross-reference convention section defines only '§ N.M' for sections and says 'the appendix's figures carry A.N' — it does not specify a figure cross-reference form. The internal inconsistency between 'figure 1.1' (label) and 'Fig 1.2' (reference) is a recurring pattern across the document: e.g., page 17 'Fig 2.1', page 148 'Fig 6.1'. The book should pick one form.
fix_instruction: Standardize all figure cross-references to one form (e.g., 'Fig. 1.2') and state the convention in the Preface reading-conventions paragraph alongside the § convention.

evidence: Page 79, §4.3 'Latency from SLO': "TTFT (time-to-first-token): budget of 1.2 s, comprising retrieval (~120 ms for vector search and reranking on a local GPU) + prefill (budget cap 1.08 s…)". The reading-conventions paragraph (page 18) states: "TTFT and time-to-first-token are used interchangeably; so are RAG and retrieval-augmented-generation. Prefill latency is not interchangeable with TTFT: prefill is a component of, not identical to, the user-observed TTFT."
issue: The TTFT_e2e convention (page 18): 'TTFTe2e = retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill' — where prefill includes sampling of the first token — is used consistently. However on page 15, the timing convention states: "prefill = processing the prompt + sampling token 1, and decode = the per-token loop that begins with token 1 as its first input." Under this convention, time-to-first-token ends at the moment token 1 is *sampled* (produced), not at the moment it becomes the *input* to decode. But the definition of decode as beginning with token 1 as input means token 1's K/V is computed during decode step 1 — so time-to-first-token ends *before* token 1's K/V exists. This is internally consistent, but the reading-conventions paragraph says 'TTFT and time-to-first-token are used interchangeably' — the two terms are literally the same phrase split across a hyphen. The sentence is tautological (it asserts a synonym that is just a line-break variant), which may be a formatting artifact rather than a meaningful convention statement.
fix_instruction: If the intent is to tell the reader that 'TTFT' and 'time-to-first-token' (unhyphenated) are the same abbreviation spelled out, state that explicitly: 'TTFT and its unhyphenated expansion "time to first token" are used interchangeably.' As written, the sentence reads as if two different terms are synonyms.

evidence: Page 100, §5.3(b): "prefill dominates the linear FLOP budget (~97% of tokens and linear FLOPs) while decode dominates single-stream wall-clock (~85% of 7.08 s on the illustrative 20 ms/token basis… ~87% of 8.58 s on the canonical 25 ms/token basis…) — the two percentages are the same quantity at two different operating points, not one series".
issue: The text says 'the two percentages are the same quantity at two different operating points' — but 85% and 87% are wall-clock shares of decode under two different TPOT budgets (20 ms/token vs 25 ms/token). They are the same *metric* (decode share of total request time) at two *operating points*, which the text correctly states. However, the parenthetical already says 'not one series' — and then the main sentence says 'the same quantity' — these two clauses say slightly different things ('not one series' implies they shouldn't be trended together; 'same quantity' implies they are directly comparable). The double qualification ('same quantity… not one series') is redundant and slightly confusing in sequence.
fix_instruction: Simplify to one qualifier: 'the two percentages are decode shares at two different operating points and should not be compared as if they were one series' — or delete the redundant second qualifier.

evidence: Canonical Workload box, 'Mean request service time' row: "~10 s [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] — an author-chosen round planning headline… It is also NOT the W used in any Little's-law occupancy computation — using ~10 s would give occupancies of 100/400, exactly the active-user population this box separates."
issue: The row says 'using ~10 s would give occupancies of 100/400' — but 10 × 10 = 100 and 40 × 10 = 400, which equals the active-user population (100 at 5%, 400 at 20%). The text implies this is a *problem* (it conflates people with requests). The confusion is that the planning headline (~10 s) *happens* to produce the same numbers as the active-user counts — not because they are the same quantity, but because the scenario inputs were chosen such that 10 × 10 = 100 = 5% × 2000. A reader might think the text is saying the numbers 'must be' 100/400 because the population is 100/400 — but the text says they *coincide* because of the planning rounding. The phrase 'exactly the active-user population this box separates' reads as if this coincidence is the *reason* it's forbidden, when in fact the coincidence is a *symptom* of using the wrong W.
fix_instruction: Rewrite: 'using ~10 s in L = λW would give occupancies of 100/400 — numerically identical to the active-user population, which is exactly the conflation this box warns against (population ≠ occupancy).' Make clear that the coincidence is a warning sign, not the reasoning.

evidence: Page 98, §5.3(a): "~186–371 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at ~30–60 GFLOP/s sustained… but only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU". Deltas: 14.08 − 2.94 = 11.14 GFLOP. Check: 11.14 ÷ 30 = 0.3713 s = 371 ms ✓; 11.14 ÷ 60 = 0.1857 s = 186 ms ✓; 11.14 ÷ 10,000,000 = 0.001114 s = 1.11 ms ✓.
issue: The arithmetic checks out for all three values (371 ms, 186 ms, 1.1 ms). No arithmetic defect. However, the text states 'single-core encoding fits only above ≈92.8 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s)' — check: 11.14 ÷ 0.12 = 92.83 GFLOP/s ✓. The threshold is correctly derived. The [HYPOTHESIS] label on the original latency claim is appropriate since no measurement is cited. No defect in this passage — arithmetic verified and label appropriate.
fix_instruction: No fix needed; arithmetic and labels verified correct.

evidence: Page 136, §7.3.1: "Device capacities are first-party specifications (Intel Arc Pro B70 datasheet, B65 datasheet, Arc Pro B60 datasheet, retrieved 2026-10-28 — post-cutoff addendum v20260913+addendum-20261028, outside the book's 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff, admitted as dated device-capacity documentation and not as a refresh of the August comparison…)".
issue: The source is properly identified and the post-cutoff addendum is properly declared. The sentence is very long (one sentence spanning ~120 words with two parentheticals) — a prose-clarity concern under ASD-STE100. The sentence mixes three topics: (a) which datasheets, (b) retrieval date, (c) addendum policy and scope limit. Breaking into two sentences would improve readability without changing meaning.
fix_instruction: Split into: 'Device capacities come from first-party specifications (Intel Arc Pro B70/B65/B60 datasheets, retrieved 2026-10-28). These datasheets were admitted under post-cutoff addendum v20260913+addendum-20261028 as dated device-capacity documentation; they do not refresh the book's August comparison.'
